The proportion of discussions documenting all core decision items rose from 48 to 81 percent. The largest gains were in the reason for departing from guidelines and the named person who would inform the patient. Meeting length did not change. The comparison was uncontrolled, and the template was introduced alongside a new meeting chair. Staff reported that the template made the recommendation easier to find in the record."},{"title":"Quality of multidisciplinary tumour board decision records: a multicentre review of 2,400 case discussions","authors":"Pellegrino-Osei A, Lindqvist-Tanaka M","year":2020,"venue":"Oncology Practice and Policy","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed 2,400 case discussions from 16 tumour boards in eight hospitals against a list of core decision items. Only 52 percent of discussions documented every item, and patient preferences were documented in 29 percent. Completeness varied more between boards than between hospitals, and boards with a dedicated coordinator had higher completeness. Minutes written during the meeting were more complete than minutes written afterwards. The review did not examine consequences for patients. Boards that recorded decisions directly into the electronic record were no more complete than boards using paper forms."},{"title":"Board coordinators and decision recording in cancer multidisciplinary meetings: a stepped rollout across nine hospitals","authors":"Okwuosa-Brandt F, Carlsson-Mbeki J, Ferreira-Holt E","year":2022,"venue":"Journal of Cancer Service Quality","doi":"10.5555/jcsq.2022.0088","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Nine hospitals introduced trained board coordinators in a stepped sequence over 12 months, and we compared documentation completeness before and after each hospital's start date, adjusting for calendar time. Completeness rose by 22 percentage points after coordinators started. The intraclass correlation for completeness within boards was 0.12. The order of hospitals was set by recruitment, not by chance, and two hospitals changed their board software during the study. Coordinators spent most of their added time preparing case lists and chasing missing items before each meeting."},{"title":"Incomplete tumour board documentation and time to first treatment: a linked records analysis","authors":"Varga-Nwosu T, Hollis-Achebe R","year":2016,"venue":"Cancer Pathways Research","doi":"10.5555/cpr.2016.0204","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We linked 3,180 tumour board discussions to treatment records in one region. After adjustment for tumour site, stage and age, discussions with incomplete decision documentation were followed by first treatment a median of 7 days later than discussions with complete documentation. Incomplete documentation was also associated with more repeat discussions of the same patient. Residual confounding by case complexity is likely, because complex cases are both harder to document and slower to treat. The analysis could not separate the effect of documentation from the effect of the board's workload."},{"title":"Patient understanding of treatment plans after multidisciplinary discussion: development and validation of a five-item questionnaire","authors":"Dembele-Sorensen K, Iwata-Moreau L","year":2023,"venue":"Patient Reported Outcomes in Cancer","doi":"10.5555/proc.2023.0059","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We developed a five-item questionnaire asking patients whether they know their planned treatment, its purpose, the next step, who to contact and whether their preferences were discussed. In 612 patients it took a median of 4 minutes to complete, showed good test-retest reliability (intraclass correlation 0.84) and distinguished patients whose clinicians rated communication as poor. Versions in three languages other than English were tested with 140 patients. Patients with limited literacy needed help to complete it. Scores were not related to the patient's age or tumour site."},{"title":"Meeting duration and case throughput after introducing structured decision templates in tumour boards","authors":"Rahman-Collins S, Achterberg-Fry D","year":2019,"venue":"Oncology Practice and Policy","doi":"10.5555/opp.2019.0141","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We measured meeting duration and cases discussed per meeting in seven tumour boards for six months before and after they adopted a structured decision template. Meetings were a mean of 6 minutes longer in the first month after adoption and returned to their previous length by the third month. The number of cases discussed per meeting did not change. Boards whose coordinators prepared the template before the meeting saw the smallest increase in duration. No board reported dropping cases from the agenda to make room for the template."},{"title":"Stepped-wedge cluster trials with few clusters: power, secular trends and analysis choices","authors":"Brennan-Adeyemi M, Szabo-Lindgren K","year":2024,"venue":"Clinical Trials Methodology","doi":"10.5555/ctm.2024.0071","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We examined the power and bias of stepped-wedge and parallel cluster designs with between 8 and 16 clusters using simulation. With 12 clusters and an intraclass correlation of 0.10 or more, a stepped-wedge design reached 80 percent power where a parallel cluster design with the same clusters reached 41 percent. Stepped-wedge designs were sensitive to secular trends, which had to be modelled explicitly, and to disruptions in data collection affecting some clusters. Randomising the order of clusters within strata of cluster size reduced imbalance."},{"title":"Feedback reports to tumour board chairs and sustained documentation quality","authors":"Lopez-Kimura E, Grant-Obi H","year":2021,"venue":"Cancer Pathways Research","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"After a documentation template was introduced in five tumour boards, three boards received monthly feedback reports on completeness and two did not. Completeness was similar at three months, but at 12 months it remained above 80 percent in boards receiving feedback and had fallen to 63 percent in the others. Chairs valued reports that compared their board with its own past performance rather than with other boards. Allocation to feedback was by chair preference. The authors call for a randomised comparison of feedback strategies."},{"title":"Recording multidisciplinary team decisions: a minimum dataset for cancer services","authors":"Cancer Network Standards Committee","year":null,"venue":"Service standards series","providerType":"guideline","abstract":"The committee sets out a minimum dataset for recording multidisciplinary cancer team decisions: the stage and performance status used, the recommendation and its rationale, deviation from guidelines with reasons, trial eligibility, patient preferences and the person responsible for informing the patient. It recommends recording the decision during the meeting and auditing completeness regularly. The document gives no publication date and describes its development process only briefly. It asks services to report completeness for each team annually and to act on items that are often missing."}]}
